title: Yahweh Will Provide — the Only Son, the Knife, the Ram
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. The heaviest chapter in the Old Testament — and the most misunderstood — falls in today's portion. So let me say plainly, right at the outset: this chapter is not telling us that God is pleased when people offer up their children. God stopped that knife. And in Deuteronomy and in Jeremiah he denounces the sacrificing of sons and daughters again and again, in the severest terms — a thing, he says, "which I didn't command, nor did it come into my mind."

And the question this lesson puts to us is one you may answer silently, inside yourself; you do not have to say it out loud. Is there something that, if God moved to take it away, your whole being would resist to the very end?

And notice this: what God asks of Abraham in this chapter is not a bad thing. Isaac is the son of the promise. He is the answer Abraham waited twenty-five years for. He is the whole joy of an old man's old age.

Let me put the answer up front. What God wants in this chapter was never Isaac's life. It is a certain seat inside Abraham's heart. And that ram was already there in the thicket all along — it was simply kept back to be seen by the man who walked up the mountain.
Verse 1: "After these things, God tested Abraham, and said to him, 'Abraham!' He said, 'Here I am.'"
Brothers and sisters, the first thing we have to deal with is that word "tested". The Hebrew is נִסָּה (*nisah*).

James 1:13 could not be clearer: "Let no man say when he is tempted, 'I am tempted by God,' for God can't be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one." So how can this verse say that God "tested" Abraham?

The difference lies in the purpose. Temptation is meant to make a person fall; testing is meant to bring a person to light and to build him up. One and the same set of circumstances — Satan's aim in it is to break you, and God's aim in it is to refine you.

And notice the kindness the writer does us. In the very first verse he tells the reader, "God tested Abraham." Which is to say: we know from the opening line that this will not end the way it looks as if it will. But Abraham does not know. For the whole of that three-day walk, he knows nothing at all.

Then comes "Here I am" — הִנֵּנִי (*hineni*). Brothers and sisters, this word occurs three times in this chapter: in verse 1 he says it to God, in verse 7 he says it to his son, and in verse 11 he says it to God again. And it is the very word Moses uses when he answers God in Exodus 3:4, and the word Isaiah uses in Isaiah 6:8.
"Here I am" is not a roll call. It means: the whole of me is here, waiting to be sent.
How can God tell a man to offer up his own son? Isn't that the very thing God himself forbids?

This is the heaviest chapter in the whole book, and it has to be taught with complete clarity. First, the text itself tells the reader in verse 1: "After these things, God tested Abraham." From the opening line the reader knows which way this is going; only Abraham does not know. Second, God never lets that knife fall — he stops it at the last moment, and he provides the ram himself. Third, elsewhere Scripture curses the sacrificing of children in the plainest terms (Leviticus 18, and Jeremiah 7:31, where God says of it, "which I didn't command, nor did it come into my mind"). So this chapter must never, under any circumstances, be read as though God would ask anyone to harm a child. Today no one may harm anyone in the name of God. There is no exception to that.
God "tests" Abraham in this chapter. So what, exactly, is the difference between testing and temptation?

The Hebrew here is נָסָה (*nasah*), and it is not the same word as the Greek behind James 1:13, "God can't be tempted by evil, and he himself tempts no one." The way to tell them apart is to look at the purpose. Temptation aims to make a person fall, and its source is the evil one. Testing aims to bring a person to light and to make him firm, and its source is God. One and the same hard thing can be both at once — the book of Job is exactly that. So the question to ask in a hard place is not "who sent this?" but "which way am I going to respond?" A practical suggestion: bring the hard thing to God and say it out loud in front of him, and then take the next step according to the truth you already know. Get the direction of your response right, and God will use that very thing to make you firm.
2. A Light from the Original: Three Modifiers, Each Pressing In an Inch Further
Verse 2: "He said, 'Now take your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there as a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.'"
Brothers and sisters, listen to the rhythm of that sentence.
"Your only son" — יְחִידְךָ. The second layer.
"Whom you love" — אֲשֶׁר־אָהַבְתָּ. The third layer.
"Isaac" — the fourth layer, the name itself, spoken out loud.
Each layer comes closer in than the last, like a knife pressing forward an inch at a time. God does not blur it over. He says every single layer of it.
And there are two things here that must be pointed out.
First, the word "love", אָהַב (*ahav*), appears here for the first time in the Bible. And the first thing it is ever used to describe is a father's love for his son.
Second, "your only son" is rendered in the Septuagint by ἀγαπητός and by μονογενής — and μονογενής is precisely the word John 3:16 uses of "his only born Son."
Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? Those two words — "love" and "only son" — stand together for the first time in the whole Bible right here, in this one verse.

And then there is the phrase at the head of verse 2: "take … and go …", which in Hebrew is וְלֶךְ־לְךָ (*velech-lecha*) — "go, go for yourself." That phrase occurs only twice in the entire Bible: at Genesis 12:1, and here.
Twice in Abraham's life God says to him, "Go." The first time it means: leave your past behind. The second time it means: hand over your future.
"Your son, your only son, Isaac, whom you love" — why pile the layers up one on top of another like that?

Three modifiers running one after another inside a single Hebrew sentence is a very rare construction. Every layer presses further into the wound. Your son — not somebody else's. Your only son — there is no second one. Whom you love — not just any child. And "whom you love" is the first appearance of the word "love" in the Bible. God does not say lightly, "Bring the boy along." He spells out the cost, word by word. There are two reminders in that for us. First, God never pretends that obedience is painless. Second, these very words come back as an echo in the Gospels — "This is my beloved Son, with whom I am well pleased." God knows what that weight is, because he has carried it himself.

Verse 3: "Abraham rose early in the morning, and saddled his donkey; and took two of his young men with him, and Isaac his son. He split the wood for the burnt offering, and rose up, and went to the place of which God had told him."

Brothers and sisters, "rose early in the morning" — this is the third time. In chapter 19 he rose early and saw the smoke; in chapter 21 he rose early and sent Hagar away; in chapter 22 he rose early and climbed Moriah. This man's way of facing a hard thing is to get up early in the morning.
And notice the order the text gives us: he splits the wood, and only then sets out. For three days on the road he carries with him the bundle of wood he cut with his own hands.

Verse 4: "On the third day Abraham lifted up his eyes, and saw the place far off." Three days. Brothers and sisters, of those three days the text records not one word — no dialogue, no struggle, nothing of what was going on inside him.
In verse 5 he says to his young men, "Stay here with the donkey. The boy and I will go over there. We will worship, and come back to you."
Notice that pronoun: "we … come back to you." Plural.
Hebrews 11:19 explains that plural: "concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead. Figuratively speaking, he also did receive him back from the dead."

Brothers and sisters, this is the arithmetic he had done. God had said, "your offspring will be named through Isaac." If Isaac dies, God's word falls to the ground — unless God is able to raise him. So by the time he started up that mountain, he had already worked that sum out in his heart.
Verse 6: "Abraham took the wood of the burnt offering and laid it on Isaac his son. He took in his hand the fire and the knife. They both went together."
In the father's hand, the fire and the knife. On the son's back, the wood. And the text says: they both went together.
Verse 7, and the question: "My father? … Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?"
Verse 8, and the answer: "God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son."
And then the end of verse 8 says it once again: "So they both went together."
Brothers and sisters, those four words appear twice. Once before the question, once after it. And set between them stands the hardest question anybody in this world has ever had to answer.
"The boy and I will go over there. We will worship, and come back to you" — was he lying?

Hebrews 11:17–19 gives us the answer: "concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead." So that was not a line thrown out to keep the servants quiet. It was an inference of faith. He believed that since God had promised "your offspring will be named through Isaac", then even if the boy were offered up, God would still have a way. This is the first appearance of resurrection faith in the Bible. And notice that what he says is that "we" will come back — he uses the plural. That is intensely practical for us: real faith does not make the hard thing smaller, it makes God bigger. He did not deny that the offering was being asked of him. He believed that God would still keep his covenant on the far side of it.
"They both went together" is repeated twice. Is that deliberate?

Yes. It stands once in verse 6 and once in verse 8, and between the two of them sits the most painful conversation in the chapter: "Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" — and the father's answer, "God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." Hebrew narrative loves this kind of repetition as a frame: it sets the heaviest exchange in the middle of it. And what makes those few words break your heart is that at that moment only the father knew what was about to happen. This picture is played out again later on another hill — a father and a son walking together — and that time nobody stopped the knife.

Verses 9 and 10: "They came to the place which God had told him of. Abraham built the altar there, and laid the wood in order, bound Isaac his son, and laid him on the altar, on the wood. Abraham stretched out his hand, and took the knife to kill his son."
Brothers and sisters, I want to point out here something that is constantly passed over: Isaac was not a small child.

He could carry enough wood to burn a whole burnt offering. He could walk three days of hill country. Jewish tradition mostly reckons that he was already in his twenties by then, and that Abraham was over a hundred.
Which is to say: if he had struggled, that old man could never have bound him.
The text records no resistance from him whatsoever. That silence is itself the deepest layer in the chapter.
So this is not only a father's faith. This is a father and a son walking together.
Verses 11 and 12: "Yahweh's angel called to him out of the sky, and said, 'Abraham, Abraham!' He said, 'Here I am.' He said, 'Don't lay your hand on the boy or do anything to him.'"
God called his name twice. And what he said was, "Don't lay your hand on the boy" — the knife was stopped.
Verse 13: "Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and saw that behind him was a ram caught in the thicket by his horns."

Brothers and sisters, how long had that ram been standing there? The text does not say. But it was not created in that instant — it was already in the thicket, its horns caught fast, unable to get away.
God's provision is very often already in place before you ever see it. It is simply kept back to be seen by the person who walks up the mountain.
Verse 14: "Abraham called the name of that place 'Yahweh Will Provide'. As it is said to this day, 'On Yahweh's mountain, it will be provided.'"
יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (*YHWH yireh*) — literally, "Yahweh will see." And the translations render it "will provide", because in Hebrew God's seeing is his providing. For him, to see a thing is to supply it.

And I want you to notice this. What Abraham said was "the lamb" (verse 8); what God provided was "a ram" (verse 13). That lamb would have to wait until John 1:29, when John the Baptist points at the Lord Jesus and says, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
The sentence he spoke that day took two thousand years to come true in full.
"Yahweh Will Provide" is often preached as "God is going to supply whatever I want." Is that right?

יְהוָה יִרְאֶה (*Yahweh yireh*) means, literally, "Yahweh will see", and from that comes "will provide." So the core of it is this: he sees first, and then he provides. What has to be guarded against is turning it into a slogan for wishing. The provision in this chapter comes when the man has already raised the knife and taken the very last step; it was not handed to him down at the bottom of the hill. And the ram God provided was offered up "instead of his son" — that is a picture of substitution and atonement, not a financial guarantee. So the healthy use of it runs like this: on the road of obeying to the end, God will see and God will provide; and what he provides is his to decide. This verse went on to become the name of that mountain, and a saying among the people of Israel for generations: "On Yahweh's mountain, it will be provided."
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first, and the most urgent of them all: preaching this chapter as though God were pleased when people offer up their children. God stopped that knife, and Leviticus 18:21, Jeremiah 7:31 and Jeremiah 19:5 declare with one voice that he never commanded such a thing and it never came into his mind. And let me say this even more heavily than that. Today not one person may say "God told me to do this" and harm anybody. If someone says that to your face, tell him straight out: that is not God — God has already stopped that knife.

The second is preaching "Yahweh Will Provide" as a slogan for getting money. The original setting of that phrase is an altar, wood and a knife — and only then a ram. It is what a father said out of the deepest pain of his life. Shrink it down into a catchphrase for requesting supply and you have taken the whole weight of the chapter away.

The third is running testing and temptation together as if they were one thing. James says plainly that God tempts no one. Temptation is meant to make a person fall; testing is meant to build a person up. Preach them as the same thing and the congregation will conclude that God sets traps for people — and that will destroy their trust in him.

The fourth is preaching Abraham's faith and never preaching Isaac's obedience. A young man in his twenties could have pushed a man of over a hundred aside, and he did not struggle. Preach only the greatness of the father and you have missed the clearer foreshadowing altogether — what stands here is a father and a son walking together.

The fifth is making the geography of Moriah more certain than the text does. 2 Chronicles 3:1 states plainly that Solomon built the temple on Mount Moriah in Jerusalem; that line is clear. Whether Golgotha also stood in that same area, Scripture does not say outright, and we will not force the point. There is no need, for the sake of effect in a sermon, to preach an inference as though it were settled fact — this passage has quite enough force of its own.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: Chinese parents hold their children dearer than their own lives, and when they hear this chapter it is very hard on them — some are even frightened by it. Is God going to take my child too? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be answered very gently. First, here is what the text actually says: God stopped the knife, and from the very beginning he never intended that thing to happen — verse 1 already told us, "God tested Abraham." Second, what this chapter wants is not Isaac's life; it is that seat. A parent can pray like this: "Lord, I place my child in your hands" — and that is not handing over his life, it is admitting that he was never mine to begin with. Third, let me draw a very practical distinction. When you put a child in God's place, the one who ends up suffering is usually the child. A child who has to carry the entire meaning of his parents' lives cannot bear that weight. When you lay him on the altar, what you are actually doing is lifting him out from under a burden he was never able to carry.

The second question: Chinese culture speaks of filial piety, and here is a son obeying his father to this extreme — will that be used to justify absolute submission inside a family? Brothers and sisters, this one has to be said clearly, because it genuinely has been misused. First, the one Isaac finally obeys is God, not his father's personal will — this was commanded by God's own mouth, and God himself stepped in and stopped it. Second, Scripture has never taught that children must obey every demand a parent makes. Ephesians 6:1 says, "Children, obey your parents in the Lord" — and "in the Lord" is a boundary. Four verses later the same passage goes on, "You fathers, don't provoke your children to wrath." Third, and most practical of all: any relationship that demands absolute obedience, forbids questions and refuses to be examined is not this chapter. In this chapter the son is allowed to ask — in verse 7 he does ask, "Where is the lamb for a burnt offering?" — and his father answers him. A home where a child is not allowed to ask questions looks nothing like this chapter.
The thing I would least like to give up — how do I know whether I am meant to hand it over?

Let me be clear first: God does not take it away every time. Chapter 22 ends with Isaac walking home alive. So the heart of "handing it over" is not loss; it is a transfer of sovereignty — swapping "this is mine and nobody may touch it" for "this is yours, and you may arrange it however you please." Three questions will help you tell. First: if this thing were gone, could I still go on believing? Second: have I ever done something I should not have done in order to keep hold of it? Third: has it started giving orders inside me in God's place? Answer yes to two out of the three, and that is very probably the thing. And in practice, begin with one concrete action: say its name out loud in prayer, and hand it over to God.
7. Living 321 Out — Laying Even the Most Precious Thing on the Altar
Brothers and sisters, let us tie this lesson back into the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Isaac carried the wood up the mountain, and two thousand years later another only Son carried a cross up that same range of hills. And here is where the two part company: Abraham's hand was stopped, and the Father's hand was not. Romans 8:32 says, "He who didn't spare his own Son, but delivered him up for us all, how would he not also with him freely give us all things?" Brothers and sisters, my role model is this: he is himself the ram, lying on the altar in my place.

The Bible is my standard — and the standard this chapter gives us is an order of things: God gives first, and then God has the right to ask. Isaac was God's gift, and so God had the right to ask for him back. Everything in your hands — your health, your family, your work, your gifts — comes from that same source. The standard is not asking you to become hard-hearted. It is asking you to remember where the ownership lies.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — and notice that of those three days on the road the text records not a single sentence. There is a kind of walking together that is silent. If your prayers lately have seemed to go unanswered, that does not necessarily mean God has walked away. It may well mean you are somewhere in the middle of those three days.

Let Jesus be King — in verse 12 God says, "For now I know that you fear God, since you have not withheld your son, your only son, from me." Brothers and sisters, letting Jesus be King means laying even the most precious thing you have on the altar. And here is something very important that I want to say: laying it on the altar is not the same as losing it. Isaac came back down that mountain alive. But from that day on the position was different — he was no longer the centre of Abraham's world; he had returned to his own place, the place of a son.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — the name given to that place in verse 14 is not "Abraham's Faith". It is "Yahweh Will Provide". He did not put up a stone to commemorate his own obedience; he gave the name of that place to God.

Establish God's system — Moriah later became the mountain the temple stood on. Brothers and sisters, one man's obedience on a hillside became the place where a whole nation worshipped. Establishing God's system very often begins exactly like this: with one person, on a mountain where nobody is watching, handing over the thing he treasures most.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We talk a great deal about denying of self and about selflessness, and this chapter gives that language its heaviest content and, at the very same time, its strictest boundary. The content is this: selflessness is not handing God something that hardly matters; it is handing over "your only son, whom you love." The boundary is this: the only one to whom this may ever be done is God, and God will stop the knife. If anyone, under any spiritual pretext whatsoever, asks you to hand over your child, your marriage, your health or your whole life to himself or to an organisation, that is not this chapter. The way to tell is perfectly clear: God stopped the knife. People do not.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, the Same Mountain
Brothers and sisters, one and the same Mount Moriah, falling into four different hearts, gives four completely different sights.

The proud heart says, "I too am willing to offer God everything." This heart finishes the chapter deeply moved, and quietly puts itself in Abraham's place. Brothers and sisters, notice that the chapter records not one grand declaration from Abraham. He walked for three days in silence, and answered his son with a single sentence. People who are actually on that road generally cannot produce a fine-sounding line about it.

The fearful heart says, "Is God going to take my most precious thing away as well?" This heart lies awake after reading the chapter. To a heart like that I want to say: go back to verse 1 — "God tested Abraham." The writer tells you in his opening line what kind of thing this is. And in verse 12 the knife is stopped. What God wanted was that seat, not that life. He is not a God who has to take things away in order to prove himself.

The ashamed heart says, "I could never do it. I would resist to the very end." Brothers and sisters, let me be honest with you: I am not certain that I could do it either. And this chapter is not asking you to prove today that you could. It asks a smaller and far more honest question: that one thing — will I admit that God gave it to me? Beginning with an admission of ownership brings you nearer to this chapter than beginning by forcing your own fingers open.

The wounded heart says, "My most precious thing has already been taken from me." You may have lost a child, or a marriage, or your health. And this chapter is painful to read, because Abraham's Isaac walked back down the mountain and yours did not. Brothers and sisters, I am not going to hand you an explanation. I only want to set the sentence from verse 14 in front of you: "On Yahweh's mountain, it will be provided." And in the end that provision was not a ram; it was an only Son. Romans 8:32 says that God did not spare his own Son. He understands your pain — because that time, nobody stopped him.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, answer that question inside yourself. Is there something that, if God moved to take it away, you would resist to the very end? You do not have to say it out loud. Just admit it to God in prayer: Lord, this one thing — I know now what seat it has been sitting in.

Second, practise saying, once, "You gave me this." Some time this week, look at the person or the thing you treasure most and say it inwardly, once: you gave me this, I did not earn it. Admitting the ownership is the first step of laying anything on the altar.

Third, walk a stretch of road in silence. Find a slot this week when you listen to nothing, look at nothing and ask for nothing in prayer — just walk for thirty minutes. Of Abraham's three days on the road the text records not one word. Some lessons only happen in the quiet.

Fourth, go back and look for the ram. Think of something in your past that you were sure you would never get through, and how God provided in the end. Write it down. That ram was standing in the thicket the whole time; you saw it only because you kept walking up.

Fifth, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church this week, in three sentences. There is a story in the Bible harder than any other: God asked a father to offer up the only son he had waited twenty-five years for. That father walked three days, laid the wood on his son's back, and when the boy asked where the lamb was, the father answered, "God will provide himself the lamb." And in the end the knife was stopped and there was a ram caught in the thicket — and two thousand years later another Father's Son carried wood up that same range of hills, and that time nobody stopped it.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that the thing I treasure most was given to me by God, and was not earned by me.
I declare that I lay that thing on the altar; and laying it on the altar is not losing it, but putting it back into the position it was always meant to have.
I declare that God's provision is very often already in place before I see it, and is kept back to be seen by the one who walks up the mountain.
I declare that any voice which tells me in God's name to harm another person is not God; he has already stopped that knife.
This week I am to hand over the one thing I would least like to lose. If my heart is not willing at all, may I still go ahead and do it?

You may, and that is how most people begin. Abraham "rose early in the morning" and saddled his donkey; the text says nothing at all about how he felt, only what he did. Obedience very often moves first in the action, and the heart catches up slowly behind it. Two things to watch for. First, do not pretend you are already willing; that only presses the pain down inside you. It is quite all right to say to God honestly, "I really do not want to do this, but I am going to take this step anyway." Second, do not try to do the whole of it at once. Walk one stretch of the road — even a three-day journey is walked one step at a time. And if the thing in question touches an important relationship or your mental health, ask a pastor to walk it with you; do not grit your teeth and carry it alone.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, let it be the four words repeated in verse 6 and in verse 8: "They both went together."

The father with the fire and the knife in his hand; the son with the wood on his back. The two of them climbing that mountain side by side. And standing between them, a question neither of them dared to ask.
And then the son opened his mouth: "My father? Here is the fire and the wood, but where is the lamb for a burnt offering?"
And the father said, "God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son."
And then the text says it one more time: so they both went together.

Brothers and sisters, that question never received a real answer, and the two of them went on up the mountain together all the same. That is what faith looks like — not that every question has been answered, but that when the asking is over you go on walking together.
And on the summit the knife was stopped, and a ram took that son's place. Abraham gave the place the name "Yahweh Will Provide".

But notice this, brothers and sisters: what he asked for was a lamb, and what God gave was a ram. That sentence — "God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering" — was only half fulfilled on that day.
The other half had two thousand years to wait: until a baptising prophet stood on the bank of the Jordan, pointed at a man and said, "Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!"
On that day: the same range of hills, another Father, another only Son, another bundle of wood carried up on the shoulders.
And that time, no voice out of the sky cried, "Don't lay your hand on him."

The focus is not on what I have offered up, not on whether I could manage it, and not on how heavy that one thing in my heart happens to be. The focus is on Jesus — he is the true Lamb, and he lay on the altar in my place. Not I, but Christ.

May God bless every one of us this week: to admit that the thing we hold dearest was his to give, and to go on walking with him while our questions are still unanswered. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point of the lesson into the head, the second carries it from the head into the heart, and the third carries it from the heart into the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at mindset and goes no further.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ Verse 1 tells the reader at the outset that "God tested Abraham", and never tells Abraham. What is that arrangement asking us to see?
2. ★★ "Yahweh Will Provide" means, literally, "Yahweh will see". How is that different from treating it as a slogan for wishing?
3. ★ "They both went together" appears twice, with that conversation set between the two. What does writing it that way make you notice?
4. ★★ Hebrews says he was "concluding that God is able to raise up even from the dead". Is faith making the hard thing smaller, or making God bigger?

Leader's reminder: this chapter is a heavy one. Before you begin, say plainly that God has never asked and never will ask anyone to harm a child, and that today no one may harm anyone in the name of God. If anyone in the group has been asked, in the name of faith, to sacrifice to the point of being hurt, watch over that person with particular care.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I can hand over anything), fearful (will God actually take it away), ashamed (I cannot hand it over), wounded (somebody once asked me for what was mine in the name of "offering it to God"). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "God will provide himself the lamb for a burnt offering, my son." Then tell the group: where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ "If this thing were gone, could I still go on believing?" Follow that question and find the one thing in your heart you would least like to give up.
8. ★ Finish it in one sentence: "The thing I am most afraid God will ask me for is …"
9. ★★ This week, what one concrete act of handing over will you make for that thing? Say when you will do it, and say how.

Leader's reminder: questions nine and ten go very deep. The leader answers first. If someone breaks down over a child, a marriage or their health, stop the discussion, stay beside them and pray; never press anyone with "you have to offer it up." Follow up with them privately afterwards, and help them find professional support where that is needed.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own home, is there a person or a matter you are gripping more tightly than you grip God? What adjustment will you make this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, or in your ministry, which position is the one you cannot let go of?
12. ★★★ The rise-early practice: this week, make one act of obedience over that matter in which the action moves first — even while your heart is still unwilling. Name the one action you will take.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — tell him the name of that thing, and ask him to walk this stretch of road with you. Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a father in the Bible who was asked to offer up his only son, and who walked three days to do it. Second: at the last moment God stopped him, and provided a ram himself to take the son's place. Third: so I believe in a God who understands that kind of pain — because later on, for his own Son, he did not stop it. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the one act of obedience you will make this week, and the one thing you cannot let go of. Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to bring us to hand our sovereignty back to him, and asking him, when we come to the very last step, to provide himself.
